meta.title: Femio
meta.description: One account for a woman's whole health life.

home.heroTitle: Your health has one story. Femio keeps all of it.
home.heroBody: A period, cycle and pregnancy tracker that does not stop there — it carries on through conditions, trying to conceive, after birth and menopause, with referenced guides for every stage.
home.antiClaim: Femio is a wellness and education tool, not a medical device — and your health data is never sold. Both are things you can check, not things we ask you to believe.

shot.heading: Open it and it already knows where you are.
shot.caption: Your dashboard in cycle mode. Every stage gets its own — pregnancy counts weeks, menopause counts months and leaves the conclusion to you and your clinician.

rail.heading: Most apps cover one chapter. This one follows the whole book.
rail.sub: When your life changes, Femio re-arranges around it — it never starts you over and it never deletes what came before.

proof.heading: We would rather be useful than certain.

band.title: A window, not a date
band.body: Your next period is shown as a range with a confidence, because that is what the data supports. The softer the edges, the less sure we are — and you can see it.

late.title: No “you are 4 days late”
late.body: Cycles shift for dozens of ordinary reasons. If the window passes, Femio says so and stops — it does not run a counter at you.
late.notice: Your window has passed. Cycles shift — this is common and usually not a problem.

pattern.title: Your own pattern, not an average
pattern.body: Everything is compared against your history — including when your cycles are irregular, which is exactly where other apps give up.

sources.claim: Every claim is cited, and dated
sources.detail: — NICE, ACOG, WHO, ESHRE, linked, with the date the page was last reviewed.

eu.claim: Your data lives in the EU

portable.claim: Export or delete it, in the app

ads.claim: No health data reaches an advertiser
ads.detail: — ever. It is not a setting; there is no channel.

languages.detail: — Arabic right-to-left from the first line of code, not a layer added later.

reviewed.claim: Every guide is reviewed by a clinician
reviewed.detail: — named, with credentials, and linked to their bio.

ttcWorkup.heading: Thinking about getting checked?
ttcWorkup.body: Guidance usually suggests asking after a year of trying, or six months from around 35. It is a good moment to find out, not a verdict.

ttcCondition.heading: What you told us still counts

longTerm.heading: Looking further ahead
longTerm.body: Bone and heart health matter more after menopause. This is awareness, not a risk score — your clinician can say what applies to you.

medications.heading: Medicines and supplements

gsm.heading: Comfort and intimacy
gsm.body: Dryness, discomfort and urinary changes are common after menopause and are treatable. Nobody raises it unless you do.

teenReadiness.body: What to carry, where to keep it, and who to tell. A plan means it is never a surprise.

window.why: Cycles jump around a lot in the first few years, so this is a range rather than a date.

window.needDataNote: Femio needs two start dates before it can work out a range for you.

reassurance.heading: You’re normal
reassurance.body: In the first year or two, a cycle that is short one month and long the next — or a month with none at all — is what usually happens. It settles on its own.

worthMentioning.heading: Worth saying out loud
worthMentioning.body: Some people find it helps to mention any of these to a parent, another adult they trust, or a doctor: about three months with no period, bleeding that soaks a pad or tampon more often than every one to two hours, or pain that keeps you off school. None of them means something is wrong. They are just worth saying out loud.

followup.heading: Follow-up after your pregnancy
followup.body: You told us about a condition during pregnancy. These checks are the ones guidance describes afterwards, and they are the ones most often missed — usually because nobody offers them.
followup.glucose: A glucose test, usually offered between about four and twelve weeks after birth
followup.bloodPressure: A blood-pressure review in the first days and again around a week to ten days
followup.overdue: The usual window has passed — worth chasing
followup.note: Femio records no result and reads none. Your clinician decides what any of these mean.

moodSupport.heading: How you feel is not a verdict on you
moodSupport.body: Low mood, anxiety and numbness after birth are common and they respond to support. Feeling this way is not a failure and it is not permanent.
moodSupport.cta: What to look for, and who to tell

intrusiveThoughts.heading: Frightening thoughts are more common than anyone says
intrusiveThoughts.body: Sudden, unwanted thoughts about harm coming to your baby happen to most new parents. They are frightening precisely because they are the opposite of what you want, and having them says nothing about what you would do. Telling a clinician about them is safe.
intrusiveThoughts.urgent: If you feel pulled to act on a thought, or unable to stay safe, get help today.

checkIn.heading: How are you doing today?
checkIn.note: There is no right answer and nothing to score. Log what you feel, when you feel like it.

loss.heading: However you feel today is okay.
loss.note: Nothing here celebrates on your behalf, and nothing counts anything. Femio keeps your record for as long as you want it.

redFlags.heading: Signs to get checked now
redFlags.body: Heavy bleeding that soaks a pad in an hour · a severe headache that will not go away or changes in your vision · trouble breathing or chest pain · a fever · a red, painful or swollen leg · thoughts of harming yourself or your baby. Contact your maternity team or the emergency services available where you are. The weeks after birth carry real risks, and being seen early is never an overreaction.

reading.heading: Reading for this stage
reading.pending: Clinician-reviewed guides for recovery after birth are being written. Everything already published stays searchable in the library.

postpartum.cycleReturnNote: Femio is not showing a next-period estimate. Your cycle can take months to return and is often irregular at first, so a predicted date now would be a guess dressed up as a number. Log your first period and the cycle tools pick up from there.

about.title: About Femio
about.intro: Femio is one account for a woman’s whole health life — from puberty and cycles through trying to conceive, pregnancy, postpartum, and menopause.

points.heading: Our mission
points.body: Give every woman referenced, judgment-free health knowledge and honest tracking she can trust — in her language, on her terms.

points.heading: Learning & tracking
points.body: Femio helps you understand and track your health. It is a wellness and education tool, not a medical device, and it never replaces your clinician’s care.

points.heading: Referenced, reviewed content
points.body: Every guide is sourced from reputable medical bodies and checked by a qualified clinician before it goes live.

points.heading: Honest predictions
points.body: We show ranges and a confidence level, never a single false-certain date.

points.heading: Privacy by design
points.body: Your health data is yours — never sold, never shared with advertisers. You can export or delete it anytime.

points.heading: Arabic & RTL first-class
points.body: Femio is built for English, Arabic, French, and Spanish, with right-to-left support native throughout.

editorialPolicy.title: Editorial policy
editorialPolicy.intro: Every health claim on Femio is traceable to a reputable source, every page is reviewed by a qualified clinician before it goes live, and every language is medically correct — not merely translated.

points.heading: Evidence over opinion
points.body: Every fact traces to a top-tier source such as WHO, CDC, NHS, or ACOG. We never invent statistics or guideline positions; a claim we cannot source is cut.

points.heading: At least two sources per page
points.body: Each guide cites at least two independent sources — at least one from a leading medical body — stored and shown so you can check them yourself.

points.heading: Plain language
points.body: English guides are written at about a grade 6–8 reading level; other languages target the same clarity, with any jargon defined on first use.

points.heading: Safety foregrounded
points.body: Guides include a specific when-to-see-a-doctor section, and a clear seek-care-now box wherever a symptom can be an emergency.

points.heading: Independent of advertising
points.body: Medical content is editorially independent. Advertisers never influence what we publish, and ads are never targeted using your health data.

points.heading: Kept current
points.body: Every page is re-reviewed at least every 12 months, and sooner whenever guidance changes.

medicalReview.title: How we review content
medicalReview.intro: No health content goes live on Femio until a qualified clinician has reviewed and approved it — our system refuses to publish anything unreviewed.

points.heading: Draft, review, approve, publish
points.body: An editor writes to our page standard and adds sources; a medical reviewer checks accuracy, source fidelity, and safety framing; only a reviewer can approve, and only approved content can be published.

points.heading: Qualified reviewers
points.body: Reviewers are licensed clinicians appropriate to the topic, such as OB-GYN or family medicine. Their name, credentials, and the last-reviewed date appear on every page they approve.

points.heading: Every language reviewed
points.body: A translated page cannot go live without that language’s own medical-reviewer sign-off. Good translation is never a substitute for medical review in that language.

points.heading: Enforced, not aspirational
points.body: These gates are built into our system: reviewer-only approval, approval before publishing, per-language sign-off, and 12-month re-review dates.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.intro: Your health data is yours. This page explains in plain language what Femio collects, why, who else can see it, and how you take it back or delete it.

draft.title: Draft — not yet in force
draft.body: We publish this early so you can see our intentions before you trust us with anything. Our lawyers and data-protection officer are finalising the binding version, and the company name and contact details below are still to be confirmed. Femio is not open to the public yet.

points.heading: Who we are
points.body: Femio is the controller of the data described here. The registered company, our data-protection officer and our EU representative are being appointed now; their names and contact details will appear here before launch.

points.heading: What we collect
points.body: Account basics (a pseudonymous ID, your email if you create an account, your age band, your language) and the health information you choose to enter: cycle and period dates, symptoms, mood, vitals, medicines, lab results you type in, screening-questionnaire answers, and your life stage. We also keep the minimum technical data needed to run the site securely. We do not collect anything a feature you use doesn’t need.

points.heading: Why we may hold health data
points.body: Health data gets the strongest protection in law, so we ask for your explicit consent before the first health field is stored — and we ask separately for each purpose: core tracking, pattern insights, and research (entirely optional). You can withdraw any of them at any time without losing your account.

points.heading: How our estimates work
points.body: Our estimates come from your own logs and general cycle patterns. They are shown as ranges with a confidence level because they are genuinely uncertain; they are for learning and planning, and they are not medical advice or a reliable way to avoid pregnancy.

points.heading: Who else sees it
points.body: Only the service providers we need to run Femio, each under a written data-protection contract and only for the minimum they need. Our database and hosting provider is the only one that holds health data. We never sell your data, and we never give health data to advertisers or third-party analytics tools. Any advertising we run in future will be based on the page you are reading, never on what you have logged.

points.heading: Where it lives
points.body: Femio’s database is hosted in the European Union. If a provider we use sits outside the EU, we put a lawful transfer safeguard in place first and record it in our processor register.

points.heading: How long we keep it
points.body: Your records stay while your account exists, so your history can span your whole health life — that is the point of Femio. Delete part of it, or all of it, whenever you want; deletion cascades through our systems, including backups on their normal rotation.

points.heading: Your rights
points.body: You can see your data, export a full copy as a file, correct it, delete your account entirely, withdraw a consent, or object to a use. Export and delete are buttons in the app, not a support queue, and we aim to complete any request within 72 hours.

points.heading: Anonymous mode
points.body: You can track without giving us an email at all. If you add one later, nothing you logged is lost.

points.heading: Teens and guardians
points.body: Teen mode carries no advertising, no direct messages and minimal data collection. Where a young person is below the age of consent in her country, we require a parent’s or guardian’s consent — the exact ages and the checks we use are being confirmed with lawyers in each market.

points.heading: Security
points.body: Data is encrypted in transit and at rest. Every database row is locked to its owner by the database itself, staff access is least-privilege, and we keep a written breach procedure with a 72-hour notification clock.

points.heading: Changes and complaints
points.body: We version this page and will tell you about meaningful changes rather than quietly editing it. You can contact our privacy team about anything here, and you always keep the right to complain to your data-protection authority.

privacy.footnote: Femio is a wellness, education and tracking service. It is not a medical device and never replaces your clinician’s care.

terms.title: Terms of use
terms.intro: The deal between you and Femio: what we promise, what we ask of you, and the limits of what a tracking and education service can do.

draft.title: Draft — not yet in force
draft.body: This is our plain-language draft, published for transparency while our lawyers finalise the binding version. It is not an agreement between us yet, and the company details, governing law and liability wording below are still to be settled.

points.heading: What Femio is — and is not
points.body: Femio gives you educational content and tools to record and understand your own health. It does not give medical advice, does not tell you what is wrong with you, and does not replace your clinician. Using it creates no clinician–patient relationship. Fertile-window estimates support conception planning and awareness only — they are not a reliable way to avoid pregnancy. If you think you are having an emergency, contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department.

points.heading: Who can use it
points.body: You need to be old enough to consent to health-data processing where you live, or to have a parent’s or guardian’s consent. Teen accounts start with a safer set-up. The exact ages per country are being confirmed with lawyers.

points.heading: Your account
points.body: Keep your sign-in details to yourself, give us accurate information, and tell us if someone else gets into your account. You are responsible for what happens under it.

points.heading: Fair use
points.body: Use Femio for your own health. Don’t scrape it, break it, resell it, overload our systems, or use it to harm anyone. We may suspend accounts that do.

points.heading: Money
points.body: Femio’s core — logging, honest estimates and the health library — is free and stays free. If we add a paid tier later it will add depth and never take basics away, and we will show the price, renewal terms and refund rules before you pay anything.

points.heading: What you post
points.body: Anything you post in a community space must be lawful and respectful, and giving medical advice to other users is not allowed. You keep ownership of your own content and give us only the permission we need to show it. We may remove content that breaks these rules.

points.heading: What we own
points.body: Femio’s software, brand and original content belong to us. Guidance we cite from medical bodies belongs to them, and is credited and linked.

points.heading: Limits
points.body: We work hard on accuracy, but Femio is provided as-is, and no health information can account for your individual situation — decisions about your health are for you and your clinician. The precise disclaimers and liability limits are being drafted by lawyers, and nothing here will remove rights that consumer law gives you.

points.heading: Ending it
points.body: You can delete your account whenever you want, from inside the app, and your data goes with it. We may limit or end access if these terms are broken, or if we have to stop offering the service.

points.heading: Law and disputes
points.body: Which country’s law applies and how disputes are handled will follow the company we register, and will be stated here before launch.

points.heading: Changes
points.body: If we change these terms in a way that matters, we will tell you and give you the chance to stop using Femio.

menstrual.heading: Your period
menstrual.body: If pregnancy has not occurred, hormone levels fall and the uterine lining leaves the body through the vagina as blood and tissue. Day 1 of full bleeding is Day 1 of a new cycle.

follicular.heading: The follicular phase
follicular.body: This phase starts on Day 1 and continues until ovulation. Hormone signals help one follicle develop, while oestrogen helps rebuild the uterine lining. It can change in length from cycle to cycle — one reason a future date cannot be known with certainty from a calendar alone.

ovulatory.heading: Around ovulation
ovulatory.body: Ovulation means an ovary releases an egg. It does not always happen on Day 14 — the NHS notes exact timing can be difficult to pinpoint and depends on the length of the cycle.
ovulatory.notContraception: These dates support conception planning and awareness. They are estimates, not a reliable way to avoid pregnancy.

luteal.heading: The luteal phase
luteal.body: This phase begins after ovulation. The empty follicle makes progesterone, which helps maintain the uterine lining. If pregnancy does not occur, progesterone and oestrogen fall and the next period begins. Some people notice breast tenderness, bloating, headaches, skin changes, tiredness or mood changes — a repeating pattern may be useful to record, but the pattern alone cannot confirm a health condition.

patterns.limit: A repeating pattern may be useful to record, but the pattern alone cannot confirm a health condition. Take it to your clinician rather than acting on it.

consent.body: This screen reads your own entries back to you, so it needs the “show me patterns and insights” permission. Nothing leaves Femio either way.

empty.heading: Not enough logged yet
empty.body: Femio needs about three cycles of entries before it will say anything about a pattern. Fewer than that is a coincidence, and calling it a pattern would be a guess.

timing.heading: When things tend to happen
timing.note: The day of your cycle you logged each one.

together.heading: What you log on the same day
together.note: These appeared together. Femio is not saying one causes the other — it cannot know that, and neither can a count.

severity.heading: How hard they have been hitting
severity.note: The average of the ratings you gave, recently against before. Not a judgement about your health.
severity.evidence: Averaging {recent} recently against {earlier} before, across {cycles} cycles

notifications.heading: Reminders
notifications.desc: Nothing is on until you turn it on, and you choose the wording.
notifications.saveError: That didn't save. Please try again.
notifications.enableError: We couldn't turn reminders on for this device. Please try again.
notifications.deniedNotice: Your browser is blocking notifications for Femio. You can change that in your browser's site settings — we can't ask again from here.
notifications.neverDoes: Femio never sends streaks, never counts days you didn't log, and never tells you a period is late. A reminder is an offer, not a score.

periodWindow.label: When your next period is expected
periodWindow.note: Once, as the window opens. A range, never a single date.

logReminder.label: A nudge to log
logReminder.note: A quiet reminder that you can log today. Never a streak, never a count of days you missed.

appointment.label: An appointment coming up
appointment.note: The day before one you recorded, with the questions you wrote down.

medication.label: Something you take
medication.note: Only for entries you asked to be reminded about. Femio never checks whether you took it.

cycleSummary.label: Your cycle summary
cycleSummary.note: When a cycle ends and there is something to look back at.

discreet.label: Keep the wording private
discreet.note: Notifications say nothing about your health — useful if your phone shows them on the lock screen.
discreet.sample: On your lock screen: “Femio — open the app”
discreet.samplePlain: On your lock screen: “Femio — your next period is expected soon”

quiet.label: Quiet hours
quiet.note: Nothing arrives between these times. Femio holds it rather than dropping it.
quiet.none: Set to the same time, so there are no quiet hours — reminders can arrive at any time of day.

delivery.label: This device
delivery.off: This device isn't set up to receive them yet.
delivery.unavailable: Reminders can't be delivered yet — either this browser doesn't support them, or Femio hasn't finished setting delivery up. Your choices above are saved either way.

phase.label: Where you are in your cycle

a11y.runStart: First logged day of this period
a11y.runEnd: Last logged day of this period
a11y.likely: Your period is likely to start around now
a11y.possible: Your period may start around now
a11y.hasLogs: You logged something on this day

calendar.title: Calendar
calendar.loadError: We couldn't load your calendar. Try again — if it keeps happening it is a fault on our side, not yours.

log.title: Log
log.queued: Saved on this device. It will sync when you are back online.
log.saveFailed: That did not save. Please try again.

a11y.cycleHint: Tap again to change how strong
